newsitem.title: UK: N.Ireland talks await Blair-Trimble meeting.
newsitem.headline: N.Ireland talks await Blair-Trimble meeting.

text.p: A leading pro-British unionist in Northern Ireland said on Monday that he would press Britain to get the IRA surrender its arms to earn its Sinn Fein spokesman a seat at peace talks.

David Trimble, head of the Ulster Unionist Party (UUP), said he would make his demand in what is expected to be a blunt midday meeting (1200 GMT) with British Prime Minister Tony Blair after the Irish Republican Army declared a new ceasefire at the weekend in its 28-year campaign of violence against British rule in the province.

Trimble, in his first public comment on the truce, was sharply critical of the government's Northern Ireland office for proposing that Sinn Fein be allowed to take part in negotiations before the IRA hands over a single weapon.
"We are dealing with duplicity from the Northern Ireland office on a massive scale," Trimble told BBC Radio Ulster.
But he stopped short of threatening to walk out of the Belfast talks if he did not get Blair to agree that the IRA should "decommission" its arsenal.
The U.K. Unionist Party, one of the smaller pro-British groups, announced on Monday it was pulling out of the talks in protest.

Mitchel McLaughlin, the Sinn Fein chairman, told the BBC in reaction to Trimble's position: "It is an incredible decision to adopt that the peace process is over because the IRA has called a cessation."
He was speaking less than two hours before a Sinn Fein team arrived at Stormont buildings in Belfast, the venue for the peace talks, to occupy its offices there for the first time.

British officials allowed the Sinn Fein delegation, led by a man convicted of bombing for the IRA in the 1970s, to enter the premises where the year-long negotiations have faltered for 13 months over the decommissioning issue.

Gerry Kelly, who was jailed for bombing London's Old Bailey court complex in 1972, said he and his aides had come to occupy their offices after the IRA ceasefire and hoped to hold preliminary talks with other parties to the negotiations.
Kelly is a senior official in Sinn Fein. He escaped from a British jail in the 1980s,was extradited from the Netherlands and has been on the party's negotiating team ever since.

The moment was full of symbolism for Sinn Fein. Its leaders, Gerry Adams and Martin McGuinness, have twice been refused entry to Stormont in the past year when they tried to join the talks. Britain refused them entry and has cut off contact with the party because of the IRA's refusal to to renew a truce the guerrillas called in late August ,1994, and broke in February 1996.

But Sinn Fein's entry was overshadowed by Trimble's talks with Blair which could decide whether the negotiations focus again on decommissioning or start searching for a negotiated settlement to a conflict that has killed 3,200.
Trimble said the IRA had called the truce because Sinn Fein had been given to understand by Britain that it would not have to secure the handover of any IRA arms during the talks.
"They (Sinn Fein) interpret is as a guarantee that they don't have to carry out any decommissioning at all," he said.

But he insisted that the Downing Street Declaration by Britain and Ireland in December, 1993, which underpins the peace process says only parties which repudiate violence and have ended it for good can be admitted.

Under this definition, Sinn Fein would be disqualified from the negotiations because the IRA ceasefire statement did not say it was a permanent ceasefire and the guerrillas hold a huge stock of guns to contest any settlement they dislike, he said.

Mitchel McLaughlin, the Sinn Fein chairman, said every party should be free to interpret the decommissioning proposal, which will be voted on on Wednesday, but he wanted arms surrender to be part of a final settlement.

"Each party will bring their own analysis to the range of constitutional and political matters also. Sinn Fein's view is that we will have decommissioning as part of a comprehensive negotiated agreement," he told the BBC.
